extracted.intended_audience: researchers and graduate students in experimental psychology of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical criteria for designing, administering, and analyzing experiments that test context/priming effects on humor appreciation (incongruity-resolution vs nonsense structures). Emphasizes stimulus selection, measurement (funniness/aversiveness), personality predictors, and statistical controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priming to manipulate salience
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular context effect predictions are operationalized by manipulating the salience of a specific aspect of the humor stimuli through the priming of that characteristic; the prime stimulus affects the processing of the subsequent test stimulus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enhancing the salience of a common aspect of the stimuli should increase appreciation for like stimuli. Isolate an aspect of stimuli and increase its salience via priming to test its effect on humor appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content salience (Goldstein et al.)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 'salience hypothesis' priming a particular humor content establishes a facilitating cognitive set that lowers the threshold for enjoyment of subsequent humor stimuli of the same theme, positively related to both humor appreciation and comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated presentation or manipulation of theme can increase perceived salience and thus funniness ratings; use content-priming manipulations to test content effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context effect hypothesis (Forabosco)
rubrics_metrics.description: The humor response is a function of the particular construction of a sequence of jokes or cartoons: the salience of various elements that a series of jokes/cartoons have in common can influence appreciation scores across a presentation of stimuli.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider serial presentation and the configuration (similarity/diversity) between items in a series when evaluating humor appreciation; test serial arrangement effects experimentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drive-reduction/Freudian prediction (alternative theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freudian view suggests sexual or aggressive content is the primary element in humor appreciation because of its effect on motivation — humor provides an outlet for drive reduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as a competing theoretical prediction to cognitive/context accounts when framing hypotheses and interpreting content effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual-process theory (sensitization and habituation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a series the 'interruption of organized processing' by incongruity may produce arousal accumulation (sensitization) that increases funniness, but habituation can counteract this once sensitization reaches saturation, leading to decreased appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to detect both increasing (sensitization) and decreasing (habituation) trends across serial presentations; include enough trials to observe non-linear trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between content and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Content is the theme (readily salient and manipulable by repeated presentation); structure is the degree/method of incongruity and resolution (not alterable by theme alone). Both are necessary but independent features of a joke/cartoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control content while manipulating structural presentation (or vice versa) to isolate effects; avoid confounding content and structure in stimulus sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneity and orthogonality criterion for categories
rubrics_metrics.description: "The criterion for establishing a category must be that stimuli within a category are more similar to each other than to stimuli within other categories; the stimuli within a category must be relatively interchangeable...Generally speaking, the criterion for including two jokes in the same category is that they correlate highly with each other across a large set of subjects" (Ruch et al., 1991).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate category membership empirically (high within-category correlations across many subjects); check homogeneity and orthogonality before assuming structural taxonomies (INC-RES vs NON).

rubrics_metrics.name: Funniness and aversiveness rating scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Funniness rated 0 = not funny to 6 = very funny; aversiveness rated 0 = not at all aversive to 6 = very aversive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use separate scales for funniness and aversiveness; stress to subjects that the two scales are distinct and a stimulus can be e.g. not funny but not aversive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify 'aversiveness' to participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Aversiveness reflects a general negative reaction to humor (irritation, boredom, stupidity, etc.); the English translation of a German term may be ambiguous to native speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear definition (e.g., 'distasteful in some way') and check understanding; ambiguous wording can confound ratings and lead participants to use content as a standard rather than structural reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardized testing conditions and anonymity procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardized testing conditions are crucial because situational factors (other subjects laughing; experimenter's presence) can influence responses. Subjects tested individually and privately (or given standardized group instructions), consent forms detached to maintain anonymity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test participants individually where possible; if group testing, give identical instructions, ensure anonymity, instruct subjects not to revisit sections, and debrief after completion. Record whether subjects guessed the study purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for order effects via Latin square/randomization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Latin square randomized orders of questionnaire and stimulus presentations to control for potential order effects; subdivide groups and randomize content and cartoon order so that no cartoon occupies the same position or follows the same cartoon across groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct counterbalanced orders (Latin square) so each stimulus appears in each serial position across subgroups and no cartoon-contingent adjacency repeats; check for order effects statistically (One Way ANOVA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulus selection based on prior correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: Select cartoons that are the best examples of INC-RES and NON based on correlational analyses: cartoons whose funniness and aversiveness correlate with personality predictors in expected directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose stimuli with demonstrated validity (prior dataset showing expected correlations) rather than ad-hoc selection; document selection criteria and append stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal or modification of high-salience content items
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex jokes/cartoons were removed because they load on different personality quadrants, may act as context variables affecting ratings of other items, and overemphasize one structural category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious including highly salient content (e.g., sexual material) that may create residual context effects; modify or remove items to avoid contaminating responses to other stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance number of items per structural category
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid overemphasis on one structure, include an equal number of each structure (e.g., 18 incongruity-resolution and 18 nonsense in modified 3WD scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure stimulus sets are structurally balanced to prevent biasing aggregate scores toward one structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personality scales as competing predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Include Need for Cognition (Cacioppo & Petty), Sensation Seeking (Zuckerman), and Conservatism (Wilson) as predictors and compare their predictive utility for appreciation of INC-RES and NON.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure these scales (and adapt items for cultural/semantic clarity) and include them in multiple regression and correlational analyses to test trait vs state hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire item semantic adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify scale items (e.g., Wilson conservatism items) to ensure semantic clarity for the target sample (change references like 'licensing laws' to culturally comprehensible terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using scales developed in other cultures, adapt items while preserving intended meaning; document changes and rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference score as relative preference measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a difference score between INC-RES and NON subscores to serve as a relative preference score for regression and correlational analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use difference metrics to capture relative structure preference; also analyze total and subscale scores separately with t-tests and MANOVAs to detect main effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analyses and transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses used include multiple regression, simple correlations, independent t-tests, MANOVAs, and One Way ANOVA. Note: some calculations were performed on log transformations of raw scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select appropriate multivariate and univariate tests, consider transforming skewed raw scores (e.g., log transform) before computing correlations or regressions, report non-significant analyses selectively when theory-relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit hypotheses for priming and personality effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses specify expected patterns: (1) repeated exposure to a single structural type will progressively increase scores (facilitation/sensitization); (2) switching structure after priming will reduce funniness/increase aversiveness (interference); (3) personality (Sensation Seeking, Conservatism) will predict relative preference for NON vs INC-RES.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State directional hypotheses in advance and design groups (control single-structure vs switch groups) to test these predictions over specific trials (e.g., examine the 4th cartoon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Group design: control and experimental prime/switch conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement two control groups (single structure presentation) and two experimental groups (primed with one structure then switched to the other on the final trial), subdividing further for counterbalancing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define sample sizes per condition, ensure gender balance where applicable, and subdivide groups for Latin-square randomization to control position and adjacency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess participant comprehension and ambiguous terms during testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Because several subjects asked the meaning of 'aversiveness', experimenters should supply a definition and stress distinctions; ambiguous items can undermine construct measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor participant questions during piloting and testing; revise wording or add clarifying instructions to minimize misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider sample size, effect sizes, and cross-cultural comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect sizes for personality influences are small; sample size may be insufficient to detect differences. Means were compared to other samples (e.g., French) but SDs may be unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power studies appropriately for expected small effects; be cautious when comparing across samples if variance estimates are missing; do not overgeneralize from small samples.
